items.originalTitle: Why the World’s Climate Talks Broke Down—and What Happens Now
items.author: T. Michelle Murphy
items.title: Why the World’s Climate Talks Broke Down—and What Happens Now
items.summary: COP31 President Murat Kurum speaks during a plenary session at the COP31 UN Climate Summit on Nov. 11, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. —Khalil Hamra—AP COP31 , the United Nations’ annual climate change summit, ended on Sunday without consensus on an overarching climate deal after about two days of overtime in Antalya, Türkiye. The annual conference brings together delegates to shape and formalize an approach to combating the effects of global warming . This year, the main dispute was whether the agreement should explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels . That commitment traces back to the Paris Agreement , a 2015 climate treaty that calls for efforts to limit global warming to 1.5°C (2.7°F) above preindustrial levels. Read more: Climate Change Is Accelerating Faster Than We Can Respond, Scientists Warn Among the countries that opposed language calling for a transition away from fossil fuels were Russia and Saudi Arabia, while the European Union, the United Kingdom, and others refused to agree to any deals that did not acknowledge the leading cause of climate change. COP31’s President Murat Kurum announced on Sunday that a deal had not been reached. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted,” he said . Australia’s Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen was a co-leader at the event, acting as President of Negotiations. “Unfortunately we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision and that’s very disappointing,” he said Sunday. Failure to reach an agreement is not unheard of, but it is uncommon; the last comparable deadlock was in Copenhagen in 2009. At the time, an irreconcilable clash emerged over which countries should cut greenhouse gas emissions, how deep those cuts should be, and whether the commitments should be legally binding. “Despite the range of expectations among states going into COP31, no delegation left believing it had been a win,” says Lavanya Rajamani, a professor of international environmental law at the University of Oxford who helped draft the Paris Agreement. For Rajamani, the impasse shows how far apart the science and the politics of climate action have become. “While such divergences are not new to the process, the gap has never been wider,” she says. The world is on track to imminently exceed 1.5°C of warming, Rajamani adds, just as governments are showing a “rapidly dwindling appetite” for difficult and potentially costly action. That puts growing strain on a summit built around consensus. What is COP31? The Conference of the Parties (COP) is the annual meeting of countries that are party to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The U.N. climate summit originated in Berlin in 1995. The host location typically rotates, with recent summits taking place in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (2023); Baku, Azerbaijan (2024); and Belém, Brazil (2025). COP31 was scheduled for Nov. 9 through Nov. 20 in Antalya, but overtime extended the summit some 50 hours through Sunday. It was the longest overrun in the history of the U.N. climate talks. Most countries sent delegations to COP31. Israel’s environment ministry said its officials would participate remotely, citing security concerns about sending a delegation to Antalya. The United States did not send an official delegation for the second year in a row. In January 2026, it withdrew from the Paris Agreement. As COP31 was preparing to open in early November, a White House official told Spectrum News that the summit “rejects reality” and said the Trump Administration was pursuing an “energy dominance agenda.” In Antalya, the countries at the table faced a different question: how to turn years of climate pledges into action. “Over the past few years, international climate negotiations have shifted from a focus on establishing rules and making promises to ensuring implementation and delivery. This phase was always going to be challenging—it is where the rubber hits the road,” Rajamani says. Broad language can smooth over disagreements, she continues, but it gets harder to find common ground when countries have to decide what to do and who will pay for it. Why did the COP31 climate talks break down? One of the biggest disputes at COP31 was whether the agreement should explicitly call for a shift away from fossil fuels. A draft released early Sunday would have been the first U.N. climate summit agreement to acknowledge that global warming is on track to exceed 1.5°C above preindustrial levels in the coming years. It also welcomed faster development of technologies that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, with the aim of eventually bringing warming back below that threshold. The draft referred back to the 2023 Dubai agreement as a whole, without explicitly restating its call to transition away from fossil fuels. “It’s unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels,” Irish Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said on behalf of the EU on Sunday. Burning coal, oil, and gas is the main cause of global warming, according to the United Nations , accounting for around 68% of global greenhouse gas emissions and nearly 90% of all carbon dioxide emissions. That warming is making heat waves more intense and causing sea levels to rise. “The question is not so much what an explicit mention would have accomplished, but what its absence would have implied,” Rajamani explains. “The 2023 UAE consensus recognized the need to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems—yet subsequent COP decisions have failed to advance, or even reaffirm, this commitment.” Meanwhile, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said in its 2025 advisory opinion on climate change that failure to take appropriate action on fossil fuel production, consumption, exploration licences, and subsidies may constitute an internationally wrongful act, she points out. “The 2026 Santa Marta Initiative on transitioning away from fossil fuels is also gaining momentum,” she adds, referring to an April 2026 conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, where 57 countries gathered to discuss how to move away from fossil fuels. “Against this backdrop, omitting fossil fuels from a COP cover decision would signal a retreat from the transition,” Rajamani says. “Explicit language, provided it did not weaken the UAE Consensus, would instead have reinforced growing momentum and sent an important signal to markets and policymakers.” Climate finance was another sticking point. The Least Developed Countries group said the draft fell short on funding to help vulnerable countries adapt to climate change. The African Group of Negotiators, which represents 54 African countries, questioned whether the proposed roadmap would deliver that funding. The group was still willing to accept the draft as a compromise. Delegates rejected a separate draft decision on the Mitigation Work Programme, which gives countries a forum to discuss how to cut greenhouse gas emissions faster and where investment is needed. At COP31, countries disagreed over how long to extend the program and how closely to tie it to the U.N.’s global assessment of climate progress. Delegates ultimately rejected the draft decision. Delegates did, however, reach agreement on a “just transition” decision, which focuses on how to make the move to a low-carbon economy fair to workers and communities affected by the shift. The dispute at COP31 was over what a U.N. mechanism to support that work should do, how it should operate, and how it would be funded. The decision leaves operational details to be worked out in 2027. They also adopted separate decisions on the Adaptation Fund and the Global Goal on Adaptation. Rajamani says the overarching deal fell apart in part because some countries were more willing than in the past to reject an agreement they saw as too weak. They worry that downplaying climate damage, while prioritizing technological fixes over urgent emissions cuts and support, could undermine climate action in the long run. What happens next? Rajamani observes a “growing frustration with the time-intensive, consensus-based negotiating process,” and she says that it yields weak outcomes that are “radically out of step with the science and the scale and severity of climate impacts already unfolding.” Youth advocates voiced their own frustration at the summit’s closing session. Oumnia Anfer, a youth representative at COP31, took the floor to address negotiators. “You have let us down,” she said . “We refuse to bear the consequences of your lack of ambition.” “Some states, including those most vulnerable to climate change, appear to have reached the limits of their patience with the process,” Rajamani explains. She points out that a failure to reach an agreement simply punts decisions further down the road, saying: “All these issues will return to the agenda at the next COP.” COP32 is scheduled to take place in November 2027 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. “Parties will return for the next round of the boxing match in Addis Ababa next year,” Rajamani says. “In the meantime, growing frustration and exasperation with the multilateral negotiating process are likely to drive greater attention towards climate litigation—which has yielded far more progressive and climate-friendly outcomes, including at the highest judicial level, the ICJ—and climate action beyond the state.” Ireland and Tuvalu plan to co-host a follow-up to the Santa Marta conference on moving away from fossil fuels before COP32. Both meetings are months away. At Sunday’s closing session in Antalya, Kurum pointed to the urgency of the work still ahead. “Climate change does not follow our negotiating schedule,” he said, before gaveling the summit to an end.

items.originalTitle: Trump's top intelligence official is also taking charge of cyber policy
items.author: Alex Isenstadt
items.title: Trump's top intelligence official is also taking charge of cyber policy
items.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will also serve as acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation to lead the office, Axios has learned. A White House official said the strong support Davies received convinced Trump to nominate her to lead the office permanently rather than keep her in an acting capacity. Why it matters: Clayton, the nation's top intelligence official, will now coordinate cybersecurity policy as outages and reported cyberattacks expose vulnerabilities in America's digital infrastructure. Catch up quick: President Trump announced Thursday he was tapping Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, to replace Sean Cairncross as national cyber director. Davies will assist Clayton as a senior adviser in the Office of the National Cyber Director until she is confirmed. Trump has increasingly turned to Clayton. He became director of national intelligence in August, and then Trump named him AI czar coordinating the government's approach to AI. Now he will temporarily lead the office responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy. What they're saying: "I'm excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next National Cyber Director," Clayton said in a statement to Axios. "I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate." The big picture: Two critical national security roles will temporarily fall under one official as President Trump shakes up his cybersecurity team amid the growing threat of AI-powered attacks. The disruptions have raised concerns about the vulnerability of the nation's digital infrastructure, although administration officials say there is no evidence they were caused by coordinated cyberattacks. Clayton himself has played a prominent role in the administration's response, telling lawmakers Wednesday that the outages appeared to stem from unrelated technical problems and system upgrades. Driving the news: Clayton spent Sunday morning on CNN's "State of the Union," ABC's "This Week" and "Fox News Sunday," explaining recent technology disruptions and national security concerns. On CNN, he warned that Americans should expect more "glitches, gaps, interruptions in service" as government agencies and businesses modernize their systems. On ABC, Clayton maintained that recent widespread outages were neither coordinated nor state-sponsored, but declined to discuss reported cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture. On Fox News, he said AI is giving malicious actors more powerful tools and warned that critical infrastructure will need upgrades. Zoom in: Davies oversees the Pentagon's information technology and cybersecurity strategy, including efforts to modernize aging systems and protect military networks. She has nearly two decades of technology experience, including senior roles at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays Africa, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens. Behind the scenes: Clayton has already worked closely with the Office of the National Cyber Director, National Security Council, National Security Agency and other agencies through his AI leadership role, according to the White House official.

Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., as Senate majority leader. "Israel is just one issue in a whole host of reasons Van Hollen is the right leader for our times. We need Justice, we need leadership that follows the will of the people not entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties," Ruffalo wrote on X . "Does not follow entrenched fossil fuel and corporate interests, nor throws a blind eye to the hard realties [sic] we face today." The four-time Academy Award nominee argued that Van Hollen had the integrity, strength and spirit to fight "the social and moral corruption that has set in with age-old presumptions" in the incoming Democratic-led Congress. BILL MAHER BLASTS DEMOCRATIC PARTY, SAYS IT IS FINE WITH RELIGION 'AS LONG AS THAT FAITH ISN’T JEWISH' "We have absolutely nothing to lose by replacing Sen. Schumer," Ruffalo wrote. "We can only gain more justice and freedom. Put pressure on your senators. Now is the time. Keep the momentum of this election going. Thank you, Senator Schumer, but it’s time to move aside." Ruffalo faced backlash across both sides of the political aisle for what critics viewed as a slight against Schumer's Jewish background. "Entrenched religious beliefs? Entrenched loyalties? Please elaborate, @MarkRuffalo," Anti-Defamation League CEO and National Director Jonathan Greenblatt wrote. "Which religion? Loyal to whom?" "There are many devout Senators & Congressmen with 'entrenched religious beliefs.' Chuck Schumer is not one of them," Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, wrote. "Van Hollen is far more tied to the Episcopal Bishop of Washington than Schumer is to any leading Rabbi. Guess what really bothers Ruffalo." RABBINIC GROUP ACCUSES JEWISH ENTERTAINERS OF 'WHITEWASHING ANTISEMITISM' IN MARK RUFFALO DEFENSE "Can you clarify what you mean by 'entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties'?" political commentator Meghan McCain asked. By Sunday, Ruffalo doubled down on his post, citing Schumer's 2018 comments at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) annual policy conference where he was quoted saying, "Of course, we say it’s our land, the Torah says it, but they don’t believe in the Torah. So that’s the reason there is not peace." "These are Senator Schumer’s words, not mine," Ruffalo added on X . "Schumer is entitled to his religious beliefs, but those beliefs cannot determine the rights of another people. And they certainly cannot substitute for international law," Ruffalo continued. "This is a conflict about land, freedom, security, equality and self-determination. Peace requires justice, accountability and respect for the rights of both Palestinians and Israelis." Fox News Digital reached out to Ruffalo's representative and Schumer's office for comment. MORE THAN 180 JEWISH ENTERTAINERS RALLY BEHIND ACTOR MARK RUFFALO IN PROTEST LETTER Human rights attorney Brooke Goldstein, executive director of The Lawfare Project and Founder of the #EndJewHatred movement, denounced Ruffalo's posts, calling the actor "obsessively fixated" on the Jewish state to the point of questioning members of the party he supports. "And now they’re even turning on one of their own, Senator Chuck Schumer, because apparently even being a loyal Democrat isn’t enough when you’re Jewish," Goldstein told Fox News Digital. "They’re saying the quiet part out loud now, no longer afraid to invoke his Jewish identity as grounds for distrust. The message is unmistakable: ‘He’s a Jew. We can’t trust him.'" "His [Ruffalo's] obsessive fixation on the Jewish state, his selective outrage, and his breathtaking moral relativism raise serious questions about whether his "so called activism" is driven by genuine concern for America’s interests or by hostility toward Jews," she added. Ruffalo previously faced accusations of antisemitism after he criticized the Paramount merger earlier this year, focusing on CEO David Ellison and his father's history of supporting Israel.

items.originalTitle: Dow futures jump nearly 700 points and Nasdaq soars 3% as stocks rebound from correction with Wall Street still upbeat on 2027
items.author: Jason Ma
items.title: Dow futures jump nearly 700 points and Nasdaq soars 3% as stocks rebound from correction with Wall Street still upbeat on 2027
items.summary: Investors are poised to begin a short trading week with some early holiday cheer after suffering the worst loss in more than six years. Futures tied to the Dow Jones industrial average surged 684 points, or 1.41%. S&P 500 futures shot up 2.1%, and Nasdaq futures soared 2.89%. That came after the Dow and Nasdaq notched their biggest weekly declines since the early days of the COVID-10 pandemic, while the S&P 500 saw its steepest such drop since April 2025, when President Donald Trump stunned markets with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The S&P 500 and Dow joined the Nasdaq in correction territory. Tech shares have led the selloff as Wall Street fears the AI boom is about to go bust. The downtrend began after the midterm elections handed victories to Democrats more skeptical of data centers. But the Nvidia spy scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s ouster as CEO poured more fuel on the fire, igniting additional worries that his “circular” financing deals would unravel and leave neocloud companies in its ecosystem without capital for new data centers or AI chips. In addition, revelations that China had backdoor access to high-end U.S. chips used in AI development are spurring a federal crackdown to close loopholes in export restrictions. Trump even vowed to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad. Moody’s Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi warned in a social media post that the stock market selloff could weigh on economic growth via the wealth effect, which affects consumer spending. He estimated that that consumer spending rises or falls by about 2 cents for every $1 increase or decrease in net worth over about a year. That means that if stock prices stay where they are, the wealth effect will subtract almost 0.3 percentage points from real GDP growth a year from now, after adding 0.7 percentage points in this quarter. “We’ve seen AI stocks selloff before, only for them to rebound quickly. Investors have been conditioned to buy on the dip,” Zandi wrote. “But while there are sure to be lots of ups and downs in stock prices in the days ahead, it feels increasingly like the easy money in the AI trade has been made. If so, the economy won’t be able to count on AI to be the sole engine of growth.” But the end of the year also tends to lighten the mood on Wall Street and lift stocks. While the traditional “Santa Claus rally” is still weeks away, the upcoming shortened week could provide some early relief. Markets will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday and open for just a half day on Friday. Thin trading volumes could also amplify stock rebounds. Meanwhile, Wall Street forecasters remain upbeat about 2027 even as markets are in corrections. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs expect the S&P 500 to finish next year at 8,700. Meanwhile, UBS Global Wealth Management and Wells Fargo see 8,200. Then there’s Steve Chiavarone, chief investment officer for equities at Federated Hermes, who has a year-end view of 10,000—or a 45% surge from current levels. He brushed aside this month’s midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep Congress and several state capitals. While Wall Street fears the blue tsunami will slow the AI infrastructure boom, Chiavarone said risks to the buildout are overblown. Even a slight retreat would be positive. “A modest pullback in the data center buildout could give cash flows time to catch up, easing inflation pressures and making the investment boom more sustainable,” he argued. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

items.originalTitle: Urgent warning issued to cruise passengers about strict new law in Mexico
items.title: Urgent warning issued to cruise passengers about strict new law in Mexico
items.summary: Cruise passengers are being warned they may need to provide extensive documentation for onshore activities at ports in Mexico. The sweeping law now requires adults traveling to Mexico with minors to prove their relationship to the children in the group, or face denial of service at hotels, resorts and tours, the "Royal Caribbean Blog" reported. Effective Nov. 14, 2026, an amendment to Mexico's General Tourism Law places pressure on tourism providers to verify family relationships, according to Travel Market Report . CRUISE TIPPING CHARGES ARE 'OUT OF CONTROL' SAY PASSENGERS AS COMPANIES TOUT 'EXCEPTIONAL SERVICE' The Mexican Senate unanimously passed the measure to combat child trafficking and exploitation, aiming to shed the country's status as a major destination for such crimes. "Pedophiles don't come to Mexico by chance," noted Sen. Laura Esquivel Torres, as reported by the same blog. "Starting today, we will begin to shut down these opportunities," Torres added. Fox News Digital reached out to Sen. Torres and Royal Caribbean for additional information. POPULAR CRUISE LINE'S BIKINI CRACKDOWN COULD SURPRISE PASSENGERS AT ISLAND PORTS Tourism operators are legally required to check documents and must notify authorities if an adult cannot prove legal guardianship or parentage, according to news outlet TravelHost. Travelers should be prepared to present passports, long-form birth certificates and custody or guardianship paperwork, the same blog noted. Documentation explaining any differing last names between a parent and child is also recommended. Even if cruise passengers are only stopping in a Mexican port for the day, the rules apply to all local services. 11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP While simply disembarking from a cruise ship might not trigger a document check, booking a beach club day pass, a local snorkeling excursion or renting a vacation home likely will, the blog reported (it is not affiliated with Royal Caribbean). Travelers are urged to call hotels and tour operators in advance to confirm paperwork requirements. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The Mexican government has not yet released an official checklist, but travel experts advise bringing a folder with these documents, according to the same blog: Travelers have been taking to Reddit to weigh in on the new rules. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "This is going to be a mess," one person wrote. "There has been no formal guidance given by the Mexican government on what will be accepted and different hotels (including different people at the same hotel) have been giving different answers," the same commenter added. "Bring all government docs and letters from parent authorizing you to have [temporary] guardianship of their kids for travel," another Reddit user said. "Not that hard, really." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "I own a travel agency and [before that] was a Spanish teacher for 17 years. [I] traveled to Mexico with my students every summer and I always had a form for this — they used to often check," a third Reddit user said. Another chimed in, "My only issue with using the birth [certificate] proof is that a passport and birth certificate are often the only, or certainly the two most important identity documents, a child has. Having both lost or stolen while out of the country would be very stressful to deal with." "I also don’t understand why it matters for hotels," the Reddit user added. Fox News Digital reached out to the Mexican Embassy in the United States, Mexico's Secretariat of Tourism and World Vision Mexico for more information.

items.originalTitle: Milky Way simulation reaches record resolution with the help of three supercomputers
items.title: Milky Way simulation reaches record resolution with the help of three supercomputers
items.summary: A team of researchers, including those from the University of Tokyo, have developed a new way to model the Milky Way at a level of detail never achieved before. They simulated the entire galaxy down to the level of individual stars by combining the power of some of the world's most powerful supercomputers using an AI-accelerated model that works on a variety of hardware platforms. Their methods can improve our understanding of galactic evolution.

items.summary: Anthony Clark's official cause of death was due to septic shock, according to a death certificate obtained by People magazine. He was 62. The "Yes, Dear" star died on Tuesday, Nov. 10. Influenza A and chronic alcoholism were included as underlying conditions, the outlet reported. In addition, acute kidney failure was listed as a significant contributing factor in Clark's death. 'YES, DEAR' STAR ANTHONY CLARK DEAD AT 62 "Anthony was one of the funniest and most talented comedians and actors I have ever had the pleasure of watching," his longtime manager, Barry Katz, told Fox News Digital. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "It was an honor to represent him and he will be missed for the joy, happiness, and love he brought to everyone he worked with and the audiences that were blessed to see his undeniable performances." Clark's "Yes, Dear" co-star, Mike O'Malley, initially shared the news of his death in a tribute posted on X. Deadline then reported that Clark died of "complications related to pneumonia and the flu." PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE "Anthony Clark died yesterday. He was a hilarious guy," O'Malley wrote. "When my wife Lisa and I were dating back in the mid-nineties, Anthony was already famous in Boston, regularly selling out comedy shows. The first time we saw him at The Comedy Connection, we laughed and laughed and laughed. STACY KEACH DEAD AT 85 AS ‘MIKE HAMMER’ STAR’S WIFE SHARES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE "He was so unique — one of those comics who is laughing along with you at the absurdity of his stories and observations. I was a fan before I was a friend. We spoke on the phone three weeks ago. He had us laughing loudly once again. Attached are some snapshots from our last episode of Yes Dear, which ended 20 years ago after 122 episodes. Rest in peace. Tony." Born in 1964, the Virginia native kickstarted his career in comedy at an early age. In 1986, Clark, who graduated from Emerson College with a mass communication degree, won a national college comedy award. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? His biggest success, however, came with "Yes, Dear," which ran from 2000 to 2006 alongside O’Malley, Jean Louisa Kelly and Liza Snyder. His film credits include "Dogfight," "The Thing Called Love" and "The Rock." He also appeared on "Ellen" and hosted the fourth season of "Last Comic Standing" in 2006. items.originalTitle: Chiefs and Bills take care of business ahead of the NFL’s biggest regular-season game
items.title: Chiefs and Bills take care of business ahead of the NFL’s biggest regular-season game
items.summary: Sunday in the NFL felt a little like November in the SEC for the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills. You know how SEC teams like to schedule a late-season cupcake as a tune-up before the big rivalry game? Well, the Chiefs and Bills don’t get to pick their opponents, but whoever put together the Week 11 schedule did them both a favor. When I wrote about the Week 11 betting lines Thursday, Buffalo was favored by 16.5 points and Kansas City by 15.5. Both covered those numbers. The Bills beat the Miami Dolphins, 26-9, while the Chiefs demolished the Arizona Cardinals, 34-7. Of course, the analogy only works if the cupcake leads into a big rivalry game. And that’s exactly what’s in store for NFL fans on Thanksgiving night, when Patrick Mahomes and the 8-2 Chiefs head to Buffalo to face Josh Allen and the 9-1 Bills. The Bills have never hosted a game on Thanksgiving, and for their first one, they get the biggest game of the NFL regular season. Sure, Chiefs-Bills doesn’t have the history of Steelers-Browns, Cowboys-Eagles or Packers-Lions. But try telling someone in Buffalo that Kansas City isn’t a rival. Mahomes and Allen met in the playoffs four times in five seasons, twice with a trip to the Super Bowl on the line. The Chiefs ended the Bills’ season all four times. And I’m guessing nobody in Buffalo needs me to explain what "13 seconds" means. DK METCALF DISQUALIFIED FROM STEELERS GAME FOR UNSPORTSMANLIKE PENALTIES INCLUDING POKING OPPONENT'S FACEMASK Kansas City certainly looked ready Sunday. Travis Kelce had a vintage Kelce game, catching six passes for 74 yards and two touchdowns, both before halftime. Mahomes threw for 324 yards and three scores, and rookie running back Emmett Johnson added 105 yards and a touchdown on the ground. That’s three straight games with at least 34 points for the Chiefs. Buffalo, meanwhile, won by 17 on a day when Allen threw two interceptions and didn’t run the ball once. How often do you get to say that about a Bills win? Allen still threw for 304 yards, and Miami managed three field goals. I wouldn’t count on Mahomes being quite that accommodating. The Bills have won five straight regular-season games against the Chiefs. A sixth would put Buffalo at 10-1, two games ahead of Kansas City. If the Chiefs win, they’ll close out Thanksgiving night tied with Buffalo at 9-2 and holding the head-to-head tiebreaker. That’s a pretty big swing for a Bills team trying to earn the AFC’s No. 1 seed for the first time in the Josh Allen era. Allen has won all three of his regular-season trips to Arrowhead and lost all three of his playoff games there. Mahomes has won in Buffalo in January, too, beating the Bills 27-24 in the divisional round after the 2023 season. But both times these two played for the AFC championship, Buffalo had to go to Kansas City. A win Thursday gives Allen a much better shot at making Mahomes get on a plane in late January. And if you’re wondering what happened the last time Buffalo did earn the No. 1 seed, the 1993 Bills won the AFC championship game at home, 30-13. The team they beat to get to the Super Bowl? The Kansas City Chiefs. BUFFALO BILLS TAP HOMETOWN HEROES GOO GOO DOLLS FOR THANKSGIVING NIGHT HALFTIME CONCERT Of course, the Bengals would prefer to host the AFC championship game themselves. They’re 7-2 heading into Monday Night Football against Washington, and I suspect they’ll be rooting for Kansas City on Thanksgiving. A Chiefs win would give Buffalo its second loss, and the Bengals don’t get a shot at the Bills in the regular season. They do, however, get the Chiefs at home on Dec. 13. And yes, the Broncos and Jaguars are in the mix for the No. 1 seed, too. Jacksonville even went into Cincinnati and beat the Bengals. But when I ranked my Super Bowl contenders at the halfway point , I had three AFC teams in the top tier. If it’s my money, I’m still betting the AFC runs through Kansas City, Buffalo or Cincinnati. So if the Chiefs win on Thanksgiving and the Bengals keep winning, Chiefs-Bengals on Dec. 13 might be the biggest game of the NFL regular season. That gives me about two weeks to ask my editor if changing "Bills" to "Bengals" and running this article again counts as plagiarizing myself. Week 11 didn’t look particularly good on paper, and most of Sunday’s early games looked about the same on TV. If the NFL wants to wash the taste of those lopsided matchups out of our mouths, though, Week 12 ought to do it. The Packers visit the Rams on Wednesday night. The Bears and Lions open Thanksgiving with a game that could help decide the NFC North, and we get Seahawks-49ers on Sunday afternoon. I’d happily watch any of those three, and none is the game I’m looking forward to most. That would be Chiefs-Bills on Thanksgiving night. The only downside is that three of those four games will be over before we even get to Friday. Then again, am I really going to complain about only having to wait four days to see Mahomes and Allen play each other? Ask me again Sunday at 1 p.m. when I’m trying to decide which game gets the main TV in my living room and Saints-Bengals is probably my best option.
